rv.q: Critic's Pick! What begins as a backstage satire of white cluelessness and Black ingratiation gradually broadens and darkens into something far more mysterious: a peculiarly American tale of lost opportunity.
You absolutely must see it if you care about Black work on Broadway, American theater, and the evolving state of our 'canon.'
Nancy Medina's revival reveals a work that has lost none of its power.
Theatre Company is putting on “Trouble in Mind” in its 740-seat Theatre with a deluxe cast led by LaChanze and Chuck Cooper, and the results are glorious to behold.
And Moodie excels as Wiletta, giving us a beautifully drawn portrait of a highly intelligent woman forced to compromise and finally bursting out of the box to tell it how it is.
An actress LaChanze proves herself to be, and not just when she’s singing, and a hell of a good one at that.

Sixty-four years late and right on time, Alice Childress' wise and stirring backstage comedy-drama Trouble in Mind is making its long-in-coming Broadway debut tonight, and to describe the play as prescient would be an understatement. Uncanny rings truer.

The story isn’t really surprising, except that now that audiences have a chance to see the play, its combination of biting humor and moments of powerfully moving drama would seem a potent formula for popular success in any era.
Trouble in Mind is an intellectually curious play, whose considerations of Black representation in art and liberal smugness make it hauntingly timely.

The work begs to be seen; it's just a shame audiences have to wait until the final moments of Act II to hear the exasperated voice of an actor fed up with a system that has minimized her enormous talent because of her Blackness.
The text still contains astonishing power; it could have been written yesterday.
I just wish this remarkable piece of writing had been given a more truthful production.
The drama – and anger – builds promisingly but an explosive denouement never comes.
It still feels radical to hear what Wiletta states so clearly and passionately about how racism works, not just in theater but as a cultural system.

Trouble in Mind may have come to Broadway 66 years too late, but in a time when the American public is currently leaning towards comfort and wanting to hide America's racist past from the classroom, the play is holding up a mirror to society, especially the sector that considers itself progressive.
LaChanze is luminous and fierce in the central role, showing us the dignity and warmth that have sustained Wiletta where others might have simply become embittered.
It feels bracingly relevant, even more so than five years ago.
It is to be regretted that Alice Childress’ Trouble in Mind had to wait this long to reach Broadway but it was worth the wait.
In the end, “Trouble in Mind” delivers a universal truth: Keeping a job too often means giving up your dignity.
Luckily, your life need not revolve around the theater to be hooked by the magnetic performance of LaChanze.
Notwithstanding, 'Trouble in Mind' is worth seeing, as it speaks directly to current concerns in the theater industry over institutional and unconscious racism.
The gravitas, lived experience, and magisterial presence she brings to the role is worth the ticket price alone, and makes a fantastic case for an immediate revival of Gypsy.

Trouble in Mind is a curious curio. It's a rather uneven play, the dialogue can sometimes be clumsy or clichéd, and Charles Randolph-Wright's sometimes overwrought direction is not a sine qua non of the art.
Trouble in Mind proves an uneven, problematic work whose history is more powerful than what we see onstage.
This Broadway premiere is long-overdue but oh-so welcome.

cn.t: Alice Childress' 1955 play finally reaches Broadway in a timely, powerful revival that critics find strikingly relevant today. LaChanze leads a strong cast in this backstage drama about racism in theater that has lost none of its bite.

vs.sum: Completed a major renovation in early 2026 with all seats replaced and legroom expanded, making it one of Broadway's most comfortable and modern houses. New restrooms significantly reduce intermission wait times.

acc.note: Elevators to all levels. 53 assistive listening devices. 11 wheelchair seats across Orchestra and Balcony.
